cases.abstract: FlexGen targets bulk language-model inference when model weights and key-value caches exceed GPU memory. It amortizes weight transfers by reusing each loaded layer across blocks of batches and offloads weights, activations, and caches across GPU, CPU, and disk memory. An analytical cost model and linear-programming search select tensor placements and batch sizes. In a simplified analysis without CPU computation, the implemented schedule is within twice optimal asymptotic weight I/O. Group-wise 4-bit compression of weights and caches further reduces storage and transfers without retraining or calibration. For synthetic OPT-175B generation with 512-token prompts and 32-token outputs, a 16-GB T4 backed by 208-GB CPU memory and SSD storage achieves 0.69 generated tokens/s, or 1.12 with compression, versus 0.01 for unquantized Accelerate and DeepSpeed. Throughput benchmarks use dummy weights; separate real-weight Lambada and WikiText evaluations show small quality changes with 4-bit compression and sparse value-cache loading, whereas 3-bit compression fails to preserve accuracy. Four-GPU pipelining scales decoding superlinearly, but total generation throughput scales sublinearly for OPT-30B and OPT-175B with 32-token outputs. These gains favor bulk workloads with substantial host memory; compression is not uniformly faster, and low-latency generation remains a tradeoff.
cases.notes: Prioritized throughput-oriented scheduling and joint weight/cache offloading, supported by the OPT-175B comparison. Retained compression as a distinct contribution and separated dummy-weight throughput from real-weight quality tests. The I/O bound concerns asymptotic weight transfers in an analysis excluding CPU computation and neglecting activation I/O, not measured runtime optimality. Table 3 supports sublinear total-generation scaling specifically for 30B and 175B, unlike 6.7B. Compression regressions on smaller models and the failure of 3-bit accuracy preservation prevent blanket efficiency or quality claims.

cases.abstract: Neural ordinary differential equations replace discrete hidden-state layers with learned continuous dynamics evaluated by an ODE solver. Training uses adjoint sensitivity analysis to compute gradients by solving an augmented ODE backward in time, avoiding storage of intermediate solver operations and making memory independent of the number of function evaluations. Solver tolerances provide a numerical-accuracy/computation tradeoff. An instantaneous change-of-variables theorem establishes that, for dynamics uniformly Lipschitz in state and continuous in time, log-density evolution depends on the Jacobian trace rather than its determinant. This enables continuous normalizing flows with density-update cost linear in the number of additive hidden units. A latent-trajectory generative model additionally supports arbitrary observation times and Poisson likelihoods for observation timing. On MNIST, an ODE network achieves 0.42% test error with 0.22 million parameters, versus 0.41% with 0.60 million for a residual network. On synthetic irregularly sampled spirals with 30 observations, predictive RMSE is 0.1642 versus 0.3937 for an RNN. Toy density experiments illustrate reversible sampling and density estimation. The memory advantage relies on reconstructing trajectories backward, which can introduce numerical error; checkpointing trades additional storage for reconstruction accuracy.
cases.notes: Selected continuous-depth modeling with black-box adjoint training as the central contribution, while preserving the trace-based density theorem and latent-time-series construction as co-contributions. MNIST supports comparable classification error with fewer parameters, not superior accuracy. Spiral RMSE concerns synthetic extrapolation, not real-world irregular medical data. Density-matching optimizers and iteration counts differ between CNF and NF, so no matched-budget superiority is asserted. The linear-cost statement applies to additive hidden units; reconstruction error qualifies constant-memory adjoint training.
